newsitem.title: USA: British Telecom woos U.S.-based MCI analysts.
newsitem.headline: British Telecom woos U.S.-based MCI analysts.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc officials spent Thursday meeting Wall Street analysts in a bid to ensure continued U.S. institutional investor suppport for BT once it merges with MCI Communications Corp.
The event, which was orchestrated by MCI, was designed to encourage brokers to pick up coverage of Concert, as the combined BT-MCI entity will be known, an MCI spokesman said.
"It's basically BT explaining their business and their strategy to Wall Street," said Barry Sine, an SBC Warburg analyst who follows MCI from New York.
"Many U.S. investors own MCI and they are going to own BT shares once the merger is done," he said.
Participating in the all-day session here were the top executives from BT's business, consumer and multimedia market units, as well as its regulatory chief and finance director.

MCI officials said the event was not designed to reveal any previously undislosed information about either company. At the event BT officials spoke in general about the opportunities for cross-fertilization between the BT and MCI.
But they declined to discuss specifics on plans for the merged company, including its strategy for boosting MCI's presence in U.S. local phone markets, analysts said.
Final regulatory okay for the merger is expected in fall.
The meeting was closed to news reporters.
Several attendees came away impressed with the candidness of British Telecom executives about the strengths and weaknesses of their various business strategies.
"I am pleasantly surprised," Sine said when asked to compare his impressions of management at BT and MCI. "You can fairly say BT has a world class management team," he said.

Several analysts said they were impressed by the efforts BT has taken in recent years to shore up revenues in the British domestic market at a time when regulators have mandated that the former phone monopoly lose substantial market share.
BT officials showed off TV marketing techniques used to alter customer perceptions that British pricing was high in order to boost the number of minutes phone users spent on the phone.
Industry analyst Jeffrey Kagan, of Kagan Telecom in Atlanta, said these marketing strategies showed BT was capable of behaving "very MCI-like."

"BT has found it can no longer rule by the old rules of the game, so it has changed the scenario," Kagan said of BT's use of marketing to sidestep the government mandate that BT cut its more than 90 percent hold over the British phone market.
"If analysts came to this meeting worried about the incompatibility of the two corporate cultures, this meeting should blow that perception away," Kagan said.
